stem: Which statement describes the nuclear model of the atom?

options.content: A tiny positive nucleus with negative electrons orbiting it
A sphere of positive charge with electrons dotted through it
options.rationale: That is the older plum pudding model.

options.content: A negatively charged nucleus with positive electrons around it
options.rationale: The charges are the other way round.

options.content: A solid ball with no smaller parts inside it
options.rationale: Atoms have a nucleus and electrons.

explanation: An atom has a tiny positive nucleus, with negative electrons orbiting it.

stem: How does an atom become a positive ion?

options.content: By losing one or more electrons
By gaining one or more electrons
By gaining protons
By losing neutrons

explanation: Losing negative electrons leaves the atom with more positive charge than negative: a positive ion.

stem: An atom that gains an electron becomes a negative ion.
explanation: An extra electron gives the atom an overall negative charge.

stem: Where is almost all the mass of an atom?

options.content: In the nucleus
In the electrons
Spread evenly through the atom
In the empty space between the electrons

explanation: The nucleus contains almost all of the atom's mass.

stem: Which particles orbit the nucleus of an atom?

options.content: Protons
Neutrons
Electrons
Alpha particles

explanation: Negatively charged electrons orbit the positive nucleus.

stem: A large nucleus is about $1 \times 10^{-14}\ \text{m}$ across and its atom is about $1 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ across. How many times wider is the atom than the nucleus?
In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What does this show?

options.content: The nucleus is negatively charged.
Alpha particles have no charge.
Gold atoms are very large.
Atoms are mostly empty space.

explanation: If most alpha particles meet nothing, the atom must be mostly empty space.

stem: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, a very small number of alpha particles bounced back towards the source. What did this show?

options.content: The electrons are very heavy and bounce particles back.
options.rationale: Electrons are far too light to turn an alpha particle back.

options.content: The atom is mostly empty space with no centre.
options.rationale: True, but that is shown by the particles passing straight through.

options.content: Alpha particles are negatively charged.
The positive charge and most mass are in a tiny nucleus.

explanation: Only a very concentrated, massive positive charge could repel an alpha particle strongly enough to reverse it.
hints: What could turn a fast, heavy, positive particle right round?

stem: In the scattering experiment, why were some alpha particles deflected through small angles?

options.content: They were attracted by the electrons they passed.
options.rationale: Electrons have too little mass to deflect them noticeably.

options.content: They collided with neutrons inside the foil.
options.rationale: The model at the time did not include neutrons; repulsion explains the deflection.

options.content: They passed near a nucleus and were repelled by its charge.
They were slowed down by the air in the apparatus.
options.rationale: The experiment was in a vacuum.

explanation: Alpha particles are positive, so they are repelled when they pass near the positive nucleus.

stem: Why was the alpha-particle scattering experiment carried out in a vacuum?

options.content: To keep the thin gold foil cool
options.rationale: The foil is not heated; air would stop the alpha particles.

options.content: To stop the gold foil reacting with oxygen
options.rationale: Gold does not react with air.

options.content: To give the alpha particles their charge
Alpha particles travel only a few centimetres in air.

explanation: Air molecules would absorb and scatter the alpha particles, so the apparatus was evacuated.

stem: Match each observation from the alpha-particle scattering experiment with its conclusion.

left.content: Most alpha particles passed straight through
A few were deflected through small angles

right.content: The nucleus is tiny and contains most of the mass
The atom is mostly empty space
There is a concentrated positive charge

explanation: Straight through: empty space. Small deflections: positive charge. Bounced back: a tiny, massive nucleus.
hints: Think about what each behaviour needs.

stem: Before 1909, many scientists believed in the plum pudding model of the atom. The alpha-particle scattering experiment showed it was wrong.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: In the plum pudding model, how was the positive charge arranged?

options.content: Concentrated in a tiny nucleus at the centre
Spread through the whole atom, with electrons dotted in it
There was no positive charge in the atom at all.
options.rationale: The atom had positive charge to balance the electrons.

options.content: Carried by the electrons dotted around the atom

parts.explanation: The plum pudding model spread the positive charge through the atom.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why the plum pudding model cannot explain why some alpha particles bounced back.

points.description: Positive charge spread through the whole atom would exert only a weak force on a passing alpha particle, deflecting it slightly at most
Only a tiny, concentrated, massive positive nucleus could repel an alpha particle strongly enough to turn it back

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What is the overall charge of a neutral atom?

options.content: Positive
Zero
options.rationale: Correct: the positive and negative charges are equal.

options.content: Negative
It depends on the element.
options.rationale: Every neutral atom has zero overall charge.

parts.explanation: A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.

explanation: A spread-out charge could not turn alpha particles back; a tiny, dense, positive nucleus can.
hints: Compare the force from a concentrated charge with that from a spread-out charge.
